intro: Marcelle Meyer plays Rameau’s Les Niais de Sologne, a portrait of the “simpletons of Sologne”, on the piano, with the first and second doubles. The theme is in D major, the first variation moves in triplets and the second puts rapid figuration in the left hand.

sections.label: Theme · Tune in D
sections.mNote: An evenly moving bass beneath the ornamented melody.

sections.label: Var 2 · Second double, left-hand semiquavers
sections.mNote: The right hand plays the tune above left-hand semiquavers.

cues.title: Opening tune over even quavers
cues.text: The right hand plays a short, ornamented tune in D major over continuous quavers in the left. Rameau marks the passage Nottes Egales, meaning the notes are to be played evenly, without the long–short inequality French players often added.
cues.evidence: Rameau, Les Niais de Sologne, Gouin edition (2005), p. 1, opening and “Nottes Egales”. Steven Devine explains the marking in his Resonus booklet, p. 4. https://eclassical.textalk.se/shop/17115/art89/4850889-2fc822-RES10131_booklet_300dpi.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The clever simpletons
cues.text: The Académie française’s dictionary of 1694 calls a “simpleton of Sologne” a man who pretends to be foolish while making mistakes that profit him. Rameau’s apparently easy tune is followed by two demanding variations.
cues.evidence: Dictionnaire de l’Académie française, 1694, “Niais, aise”, under “Nid”: the proverbial niais de Sologne feigns simplicity and errs to his own advantage. https://www.dictionnaire-academie.fr/article/A1N0043-04

cues.title: First double, triplets against quavers
cues.text: The first double, a variation, gives the right hand triplets while the left hand continues in pairs of quavers. The hands divide the same beat differently, and the tune is carried within the right hand’s quicker notes.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, pp. 3–4, Premier Double des Niais; Steven Devine’s Resonus notes, p. 4, discuss the written triplets against duplets. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/df/IMSLP132660-WIMA.e0b8-Rameau_Les_Niais.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second double, left-hand semiquavers
cues.text: In the second double the right hand returns to the plain tune and the left hand plays continuous semiquavers. The melody stays recognisable above them, and the left-hand part is the harder of the two.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, pp. 5–7, Second Double des Niais. Mahan Esfahani describes the continuing right-hand tune and virtuoso left-hand writing in his Hyperion notes. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15934_68071&vw=dc
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meyer recording, Salle Adyar, 1953
cues.text: Marcelle Meyer recorded Rameau’s keyboard music in the Salle Adyar in Paris on 29 and 30 October 1953. Les Discophiles Français issued the collection as DF 98/99.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies the venue, dates, pianist and DF 98/99 source; the Marcelle Meyer chronology lists the same October sessions and issue. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jean-Philippe_Rameau_-_Les_Niais_de_Sologne_(Marcelle_Meyer,_1953).flac ; https://classical-pianists.net/viii/marcelle-meyer/chronology/

composer.epithet: Composer and theorist who explained the roots of chords in a treatise and wrote his first opera at the age of fifty.
facts: Organist in Dijon, Clermont-Ferrand and Lyon; first harpsichord book, 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
Alexandre Le Riche de La Pouplinière, financier with a private orchestra
composer.background:
When Hippolyte et Aricie opened at the Paris Opéra on 1 October 1733, Rameau had just turned fifty. One passage had already been cut. A trio for the Fates, with harmonies that proved too difficult for the singers and players in rehearsal, was removed before the première. The opera divided its audience. Admirers heard a new theatrical voice, while devotees of Lully heard an attack on their inheritance. It was the first opera by Rameau, an organist from Dijon.

His father played the organ in Dijon. Jean-Philippe followed the same trade in a succession of French churches, with appointments in Clermont-Ferrand, Dijon and Lyon and an early attempt to establish himself in Paris. There he published his first harpsichord book in 1706. It begins with an unmeasured prelude, in which the player must work out the timing of the notes, followed by a faster section in regular metre. Allemandes, courante and sarabandes follow. He was twenty-three, and he was writing within the French keyboard tradition before Couperin had published his first book.
